title: The muscles of facial expression
summary: Muscles that pull on skin, all from one nerve, all from one embryonic arch.
objectives: Explain what makes the facial muscles different from every other muscle group
Name the sphincters and the dilators of the face and what each does
Separate an upper motor neurone from a lower motor neurone facial palsy
Separate facial muscle motor supply from sensation in the overlying skin
takeaways: They insert into skin, not bone, and all are supplied by the facial nerve (VII) from the second pharyngeal arch.
Orbicularis oculi closes the eye; orbicularis oris closes the mouth; buccinator keeps food off the cheek.
Relative forehead sparing suggests a supranuclear pattern; whole-side weakness suggests a lower motor neurone pattern, which can arise in the pons or peripheral VII.
VII moves the facial muscles; most facial skin sensation travels through V. The buccal branches of V3 and VII have different jobs.

steps.title: A muscle group unlike any other
steps.text:
Every other skeletal muscle pulls bone on bone. These pull on skin. They lie in the superficial fascia of the face, and because their insertion moves the skin directly they can produce expression rather than movement.

All of them develop from the second pharyngeal arch, and so all of them are supplied by the nerve of that arch, the facial nerve. One nerve, one arch, one plane: it makes the group easy to reason about even though there are more than twenty muscles in it.

check.q: What single nerve supplies every muscle of facial expression?

steps.title: The two sphincters
steps.text:
Orbicularis oculi encircles the eye in two parts. The palpebral part, inside the lids, closes them gently — blinking, and sleep. The orbital part, in a ring around the orbital margin, screws the eye shut. Lose it and the eye cannot close, the cornea dries and ulcerates: the reason a facial palsy needs eye protection on the first day.

Orbicularis oris encircles the mouth. It is not a simple ring but the meeting place of every muscle that converges on the lips, and it does the work of closing the mouth, pursing the lips, whistling and speech.
steps.clinical: Ask the patient to screw the eyes shut and resist you opening them: this tests the orbital part directly and is more sensitive than a gentle close.

check.q: Which part of orbicularis oculi blinks?
check.a: The palpebral part, within the eyelids.

steps.title: The dilators, and the smile
steps.text:
Radiating from the mouth are the muscles that open and shape it: zygomaticus major (the smile), zygomaticus minor, levator labii superioris, levator anguli oris, risorius, depressor anguli oris, depressor labii inferioris and mentalis.

Because they act as a group, weakness shows first as an asymmetric nasolabial fold — the crease from nose to angle of mouth flattens on the affected side, at rest, before any movement is tested.

steps.title: Buccinator, the odd one out
steps.text:
Buccinator forms the muscular wall of the cheek. It is a facial muscle by nerve supply and by arch, but it does not act on expression: it presses the cheek against the teeth, keeping food on the grinding surfaces and expelling air when you blow (its name comes from the trumpeter).

The parotid duct pierces it opposite the second upper molar. Paralyse buccinator and food collects in the cheek — the reason a stroke patient must have the mouth checked after eating.
steps.pitfall: Buccinator is a muscle of facial expression (VII), not of mastication (V3), despite the job it does.

steps.title: Platysma and the neck
steps.text:
Platysma is a broad sheet in the superficial fascia running from the fascia over pectoralis major and deltoid up to the mandible and the lower face. It tenses the skin of the neck and pulls the corners of the mouth down.

Surgically it matters as a plane: incisions in the neck are closed in layers with platysma as one of them, and a wound that has breached platysma in penetrating neck trauma is treated as deep until proved otherwise.

steps.title: Upper or lower motor neurone?
steps.text:
The upper face receives bilateral cortical input, while control of the lower face is predominantly contralateral. A unilateral supranuclear lesion therefore often weakens the opposite lower face while relatively sparing forehead movement.

A lower motor neurone lesion of VII can weaken the whole ipsilateral face, including the forehead. This includes a lesion of the facial nucleus or fascicle in the pons, as well as a peripheral nerve lesion. Forehead involvement alone does not exclude stroke; accompanying signs and the full pattern are needed to localise the lesion.

check.q: What motor pattern is suggested by weakness of both the forehead and lower face on the same side?
check.a: A lower motor neurone pattern affecting VII. The lesion may be in the pons or the peripheral nerve, so this finding alone does not establish Bell's palsy.

steps.title: Two buccal nerves, two different jobs
steps.text:
The word buccal names a region, not a single function. The buccal branch of the facial nerve carries motor fibres to muscles including buccinator. The buccal nerve from V3 is chiefly sensory, supplying the cheek mucosa and neighbouring skin and gingiva.

A person can therefore have weak cheek compression with preserved cheek sensation, or altered sensation without buccinator paralysis. The same distinction applies across much of the face: VII moves the muscles while V reports sensation. When two nerves share a regional name, trace each back to its parent before deciding what it does.

check.q: Which buccal nerve supplies the motor fibres that compress the cheek?
check.a: The buccal branch of VII; the buccal nerve of V3 is primarily sensory.

title: The muscles of mastication and the jaw
summary: Four muscles, one nerve, and the only joint in the head that moves.
objectives: Name the four muscles of mastication and the movement each produces
Describe the two-part movement of the temporomandibular joint
Explain why the jaw deviates towards a weak side
Explain how hyoid stabilisation allows the suprahyoid muscles to assist jaw opening
takeaways: Temporalis, masseter, medial and lateral pterygoid — all from the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve.
The TMJ hinges in its lower compartment and slides in its upper one.
Only lateral pterygoid opens the jaw; the other three close it.
Jaw opening combines condylar translation with depression of the mandible; suprahyoid muscles assist when the hyoid is stabilised.

steps.title: Four muscles, one nerve
steps.text:
The muscles of mastication develop from the first pharyngeal arch and are supplied by its nerve, the mandibular division of the trigeminal (V3). That is the clean division to hold on to: first arch and V3 chew, second arch and VII make expressions.

The four are temporalis, masseter, and the medial and lateral pterygoids.

steps.title: Temporalis and masseter, the closers
steps.text:
Temporalis is a fan filling the temporal fossa, passing deep to the zygomatic arch to reach the coronoid process. Its anterior fibres elevate the jaw; its posterior, nearly horizontal fibres retract it.

Masseter is a thick quadrilateral running from the zygomatic arch down to the angle and ramus of the mandible. It is the most powerful elevator, and the one you can feel bulge when you clench. Both can be felt while the patient clenches — a quick bedside test of V3 motor function.

check.q: Which part of temporalis retracts the jaw?

steps.title: The pterygoids
steps.text:
The medial pterygoid mirrors masseter on the inside of the ramus — the two form a sling round the angle of the mandible — and it elevates.

The lateral pterygoid is the one that does something different: it runs almost horizontally backwards to the neck of the mandible and the joint capsule, so it pulls the condyle and the disc forwards. Both together protrude and depress the jaw; one alone swings the chin to the opposite side, which is how you grind.

check.q: Which muscle of mastication opens the mouth?
check.a: The lateral pterygoid (helped by gravity and the suprahyoid muscles).

steps.title: The temporomandibular joint
steps.text:
A synovial joint with an articular disc dividing it into two compartments, each doing a different job. The lower compartment, between condyle and disc, is a hinge — the first 20 mm or so of opening. The upper compartment, between disc and temporal bone, is a glide: the condyle and disc translate forwards onto the articular eminence for the rest of the opening.

Translate too far and the condyle can pass in front of the eminence and stick there — a dislocated jaw, reduced by pressing down and back on the lower molars.

check.q: Which compartment of the TMJ hinges and which slides?

steps.title: Deviation tells you the side
steps.text:
Because each lateral pterygoid pushes its own condyle forwards, the pair working together keep the jaw straight. If one is weak — a V3 lesion — the working side pushes its condyle forwards unopposed and the chin swings towards the weak side on opening.

The same logic runs through the head and neck: the tongue also deviates towards a weak hypoglossal nerve, and for the same mechanical reason.

check.q: The jaw deviates to the left on opening. Which nerve is affected?
check.a: The left mandibular nerve (V3) — deviation is towards the weak side.

steps.title: Opening also needs an anchor below
steps.text:
Lateral pterygoid helps bring the mandibular condyle forwards, but jaw opening also uses the suprahyoid muscles, including digastric, mylohyoid and geniohyoid. If the hyoid is held steady by the infrahyoid muscles, these muscles can pull the mandible down.

Reverse the fixed attachment and their effect changes: with the mandible stabilised, they can elevate the hyoid during swallowing. Gravity assists ordinary opening, but it is not the whole mechanism. A muscle action depends on which end is free to move, so an origin-and-insertion list is only the start of understanding it.

check.q: Why must the hyoid be stabilised for the suprahyoid muscles to depress the jaw effectively?
check.a: They need a fixed lower attachment from which to pull the mandible down; otherwise their pull can elevate the hyoid instead.

title: The muscles of the back, layer by layer
summary: Two groups that only look alike: migrants from the limb bud lying on the true muscles of the back.
objectives: Separate extrinsic from intrinsic back muscles by nerve supply as well as by position
Peel the back in the order a dissection does
Name the three columns of erector spinae and what they do
Distinguish eccentric control of forward bending from concentric spinal extension
takeaways: Extrinsic back muscles move the limb and are supplied by anterior rami; intrinsic muscles move the spine and are supplied by posterior rami.
Trapezius is the exception: it is supplied by the accessory nerve.
Erector spinae from lateral to medial: iliocostalis, longissimus, spinalis.
The spinal extensors can control forward bending while lengthening; a muscle can oppose a movement rather than produce it.

steps.title: The rule that sorts them
steps.text:
Two groups lie on top of one another and look, at first, like one. The extrinsic muscles have migrated onto the back from elsewhere and act on the upper limb or the ribs; they keep the nerve supply they were born with, from anterior rami. The intrinsic (true) back muscles act on the vertebral column and are supplied by posterior rami.

Nerve supply, not position, is what defines them. Learn the rule first and the layers fall into place.

check.q: Which rami supply the true muscles of the back?

steps.title: First layer: trapezius and latissimus dorsi
steps.text:
Trapezius covers the upper back from the skull and the nuchal ligament to the spine of the scapula, acromion and lateral clavicle. Upper fibres elevate the scapula, middle fibres retract it, lower fibres depress and help rotate it upwards. It is supplied by the accessory nerve (XI) — the one extrinsic muscle that is not on an anterior ramus.

Latissimus dorsi sweeps from the thoracolumbar fascia, lower ribs and iliac crest up to the floor of the intertubercular groove of the humerus. It extends, adducts and medially rotates the arm — the pull-up and swimming muscle — through the thoracodorsal nerve.

check.q: Which nerve supplies trapezius, and how do you test it?
check.a: The accessory nerve (XI) — shrug the shoulders against resistance.

steps.title: Second layer: the scapular retractors
steps.text:
Take trapezius away and you find levator scapulae, rhomboid minor and rhomboid major, running downwards and laterally from the cervical and upper thoracic spines to the medial border of the scapula.

They retract the scapula and rotate it downwards. The dorsal scapular nerve supplies them; its injury lets the scapula drift laterally and wing slightly, which is easy to confuse with a long thoracic nerve palsy until you look at which way the scapula has moved.

steps.title: Third layer: the ribs
steps.text:
Deeper again, two thin sheets that belong to respiration rather than to the limb: serratus posterior superior, running down and out to the upper ribs, and serratus posterior inferior, running up and out to the lower ribs.

They are supplied by intercostal nerves — anterior rami again — and although their mechanical contribution to breathing is small, they mark the boundary: everything deep to them is a true muscle of the back.

steps.title: Erector spinae
steps.text:
Now the true back. Erector spinae rises as a single tendon from the sacrum and iliac crest and splits into three columns. From lateral to medial: iliocostalis (to the ribs), longissimus (the long middle column, reaching the mastoid process), and spinalis (the small medial one, spine to spine).

Acting together they extend the spine; acting on one side they bend it that way. In standing, they work in bursts to stop you falling forwards rather than continuously — which is why prolonged stooping, not standing, is what tires the back.
steps.mnemonic: I Long for Spinach — Iliocostalis, Longissimus, Spinalis, lateral to medial.

steps.title: The transversospinal group
steps.text:
Deepest of all, running from transverse processes up to spinous processes: semispinalis (crossing about five segments), multifidus (two to four) and the rotatores (one or two).

The shorter and deeper they are, the less they move the spine and the more they sense it. Multifidus and the rotatores are packed with muscle spindles and act as proprioceptive stabilisers — the reason rehabilitation after back pain concentrates on deep stabiliser control rather than on the big superficial muscles.

check.q: What is the main job of the rotatores, given how short they are?
check.a: Proprioception and segmental stabilisation rather than producing movement.

steps.title: An extensor can work while you bend forwards
steps.text:
Calling erector spinae an extensor describes the direction of the torque it generates. It does not mean it contracts only while the spine moves into extension. During controlled forward bending, gravity produces flexion and the extensors can lengthen under tension to brake the descent: an eccentric contraction.

When you straighten again, the same group can shorten to generate extension. Deeper segmental muscles help control the relative positions of neighbouring vertebrae throughout the movement. Watch an imagined slow bend and return: the direction of movement changes, but the same muscles may contribute to both halves for different mechanical reasons.

check.q: How can an extensor be active while the spine is moving into flexion?
check.a: It can contract eccentrically, producing an opposing extension torque while lengthening to control the movement.

title: The suboccipital triangle
summary: A small triangle at the top of the neck with an artery, a nerve and a vein you must not meet by surprise.
objectives: Name the three muscles that bound the suboccipital triangle
State its contents and their clinical importance
Explain why the vertebral artery is vulnerable here
Relate the attachments of the suboccipital muscles to movement at C0-C1 and C1-C2
takeaways: Boundaries: rectus capitis posterior major, obliquus capitis superior, obliquus capitis inferior.
Contents: the third part of the vertebral artery, the suboccipital nerve (posterior ramus of C1) and a venous plexus.
The suboccipital muscles are proprioceptive: they are among the most spindle-rich muscles in the body.
Obliquus capitis inferior rotates C1 on C2; muscles reaching the occiput also influence head position at the atlanto-occipital joints.

steps.title: Getting down to it
steps.text:
Peel trapezius, then splenius capitis, then semispinalis capitis off the back of the neck and a small triangle appears on each side, just below the occipital bone.

It is the deepest place in the neck a dissection reaches from behind, and it is crowded: everything in it is important.

steps.title: The three sides
steps.text:
Rectus capitis posterior major runs from the spine of the axis up and out to the occipital bone: the medial border. Obliquus capitis superior runs from the transverse process of the atlas up to the occipital bone: the lateral border. Obliquus capitis inferior runs from the spine of the axis out to the transverse process of the atlas: the lower border.

Notice that obliquus capitis inferior is the only 'capitis' muscle that does not reach the head. It rotates the atlas, and with it the skull, around the dens.

check.q: Which boundary muscle of the triangle does not attach to the skull?
check.a: Obliquus capitis inferior — axis to atlas only.

steps.title: What lies in the floor
steps.text:
The floor is the posterior arch of the atlas and the posterior atlanto-occipital membrane. Lying on that arch, in a groove, is the third part of the vertebral artery, running horizontally before it turns up through the foramen magnum.

This horizontal course is the price of allowing the head to rotate on the neck without kinking the artery — and it is why forceful rotation of the neck, including some manipulations, can dissect the vessel.
steps.clinical: Vertebral artery dissection presents with neck pain and posterior circulation symptoms in a young patient — often after trivial neck trauma.

check.q: Which part of the vertebral artery lies in the floor of the triangle?
check.a: The third part, in the groove on the posterior arch of the atlas.

steps.title: The nerves, and the reason for the headache
steps.text:
The suboccipital nerve — the posterior ramus of C1 — emerges between the artery and the arch and supplies the four suboccipital muscles. It is almost purely motor.

Just below, the greater occipital nerve (posterior ramus of C2) hooks round the lower border of obliquus capitis inferior and turns up over the back of the scalp. Irritation here gives occipital neuralgia: sharp shooting pain from the base of the skull to the vertex, with tenderness at one point where the nerve pierces the muscle.

steps.title: Why so many spindles
steps.text:
These four small muscles contain a density of muscle spindles far beyond what their size or strength would suggest — several times that of a large limb muscle.

They are not there to move the head so much as to report where it is. Their input feeds the vestibular system and the cervico-ocular reflex, and dysfunction here is one explanation for the dizziness that accompanies neck injury.

check.q: What does the extraordinary spindle density of the suboccipital muscles suggest about their role?
check.a: They are primarily proprioceptive — telling the brain the position of the head on the neck.

steps.title: Read the movement from the attachment
steps.text:
Trace obliquus capitis inferior from the spinous process of C2 to the transverse process of C1. Its pull turns the atlas towards the same side around the dens. The skull travels with the atlas even though this muscle never attaches to the skull itself.

Rectus capitis posterior major and obliquus capitis superior do reach the occiput, so they can help adjust the head relative to the upper cervical vertebrae. Compare their short lines of pull with the much longer superficial neck muscles. Fine positioning uses small changes at specific joints rather than treating the neck as one hinge.

check.q: How can obliquus capitis inferior rotate the head without attaching to the occipital bone?
check.a: It rotates the atlas on the axis, carrying the supported skull with it.
